analysis.one_liner: Lets companies sue to strike down state chemical warning-label laws and bars labels below strict risk thresholds.
analysis.headline: The Accurate Labels Act, which would have overridden state chemical and radiation warning-label laws, died in the Senate Commerce Committee with no vote and zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have amended the Fair Packaging and Labeling Act to set a single federal standard for warning labels about chemicals and radiation in consumer products. It would have barred states and cities from enforcing labeling requirements unless those rules met detailed federal risk-based criteria, exempted naturally occurring substances, trace levels under 0.1 percent, and trade secrets, and let companies file federal lawsuits against states whose rules did not comply. It never got a hearing or a vote; it was referred to committee and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, manufacturers, distributors, retailers, and their suppliers would have gained a federal shield against state and local warning-label mandates — most notably California-style right-to-know laws requiring warnings about chemicals linked to cancer or reproductive harm. Companies could also have withheld ingredients as trade secrets and sued states in federal court to void or block enforcement of their labeling rules.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would have barred any federal, state, or local labeling requirement about chemicals or radiation unless it met federal standards: it had to be risk-based, rely on 'best available science,' and meet defined de minimis risk levels [S2] [S3].
It would have exempted labels from covering naturally occurring substances, 'non-functional' constituents, trace concentrations below 0.1 percent, and trade secrets [S2] [S3].
It would have allowed companies to satisfy labeling rules by posting information online behind a 'Scan here for more' link or a phone number instead of on the package [S3].

It would have given companies a private right of action to sue states, cities, or citizen groups enforcing state labeling laws in federal court, and put the burden on the government to prove its rule met the federal standard — with the rule unenforceable against that company if it failed [S3].
It would have flatly prohibited states from imposing any labeling requirement 'in addition to, or different than' the new federal standard [S3].

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, consumers would have borne the cost: fewer warnings on products about chemicals linked to cancer or reproductive harm, warnings hidden behind QR codes and phone lines, and trade-secret exemptions keeping ingredient information off labels. State governments and the citizen-enforcement groups that sue under state right-to-know laws would have lost their authority and faced federal lawsuits for enforcing their own rules.

drawbacks.text: State warning systems like California's are frequently criticized for applying vague 'may cause cancer' labels so broadly that they carry little real information — a cost of the status quo the bill claimed to fix, though that claim was not tested here [S2].

The bill's remedies went far beyond cleaning up warning text: by shifting the burden of proof to governments, letting companies sue the moment a labeling law is enacted, and preempting all stricter state rules, it would have made state right-to-know laws costly to defend and easy to evade [S3].

Exempting naturally occurring substances and trace concentrations would have removed warnings for some exposures consumers may still want information about, and the trade-secret exemption would have kept some ingredients undisclosed entirely [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a fair critique buried in the bill's premise — some state warning labels are overused and uninformative — but the bill's response was to hand companies a federal lawsuit against their own state governments and to wipe out stricter state rules wholesale, rather than simply improving label clarity. The cost to consumers' access to chemical hazard information would have outweighed the modest benefit of tidier labels.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Moran introduced it on June 6, 2018 and it was sent to the Commerce Committee, which never considered it; it died there when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

narrative.text: Sen. Jerry Moran (R-KS) introduced the Accurate Labels Act in the Senate on June 6, 2018 [S1] [S5].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S5].
No further action was taken; no cosponsors signed on [S4] [S5].
The bill died in committee when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers and state governments benefited from the bill's death: state right-to-know warning laws and the citizen enforcement suits under them remained intact. Manufacturers and retailers gained nothing, but they also lost nothing.

for.name: Sen. Jerry Moran
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Accurate Labels Act and it was referred to committee.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral — no hearing, markup, or floor consideration was ever scheduled.

against.name: Public health and environmental advocacy organizations
against.role: Opponents of parallel state-labeling preemption efforts
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed the measure, arguing it would gut state right-to-know laws like California's Prop 65.

sides.party_line_note: The bill attracted no cosponsors and no votes, so no partisan split ever formed; its sponsor was a Republican and similar preemption proposals had industry backing but no committee action.

industries.industry: Consumer product manufacturers, retailers, and chemical suppliers
industries.note: The bill would have freed them from state and local warning-label mandates, allowed trade-secret withholding, and given them a federal lawsuit against states that tried to enforce stricter rules. Its gains came directly at the expense of the hazard information consumers see on labels.
Groups that sue companies under state right-to-know laws (such as private enforcers of California's Prop 65) would have faced federal suits and lost the state rules they rely on.
The bill would have barred states and cities from setting any chemical or radiation labeling rules stricter than the federal standard and put the burden on them to defend their own laws in court.
